passage.title: The Quiet Rebellion
passage.text:
My grandmother never learned to read, and for most of my childhood I did not know it. She hid it the way a magician hides a card: in plain sight, with confidence. When a letter came, she would say her eyes were tired and hand it to me. At the market she memorized prices by listening. She signed documents with a careful, looping mark that looked, to anyone not paying attention, like a signature.

I found out when I was twelve. I had left a note on the table saying I would be at Marvin's house, and she scolded me that evening for disappearing. "But I wrote you a note," I said, and watched something close behind her eyes.

She was seventy-one when she enrolled in the barangay's adult literacy class. She told no one in the family. I learned only because the teacher was my former Grade 2 adviser, who mentioned, smiling, that my grandmother was the most stubborn student she had ever had. Stubborn, she explained, in the best way: she refused to leave the room until each day's letters stayed in her head.

Six months later a birthday card arrived for me. The handwriting was large and uneven, the letters leaning like trees in a wind. It said: "To my apo. Now I can read your notes. Love, Lola." I have received better-looking cards since then. I have never received a braver one.

words.meaning: the ability to read and write
words.example: The program improved adult literacy in the town.

words.meaning: refusing to change or give up
words.example: The stubborn goat would not move.

words.meaning: officially joined a class or school
words.example: He enrolled in a swimming class.

items.prompt: From whose point of view is the story told?
items.why: The narrator says "I" and "my grandmother" and shares only what they themselves saw and learned.

items.prompt: "She hid it the way a magician hides a card: in plain sight, with confidence." What does this simile show?
choices: She concealed her secret skillfully by acting sure of herself.
She played cards at the market.
items.why: A magician's card is right there but unnoticed; the grandmother's secret was the same.

items.prompt: Which detail BEST supports the idea that the grandmother worked hard to hide that she could not read?
choices: The teacher was the narrator's Grade 2 adviser.
She memorized prices at the market by listening and used a looping mark as a signature.
items.why: These are specific strategies she used to pass as literate. The other details are about her age, the teacher, or the card.

items.prompt: "'But I wrote you a note,' I said, and watched something close behind her eyes." Nothing really closed. What does this image mean?
choices: She fell asleep while the narrator was talking.
Her expression shut down as she hid her reaction to being found out.
She closed her eyes because she was angry about Marvin.
She had something stuck in her eye.
items.why: The note just revealed that she could not read. "Something close behind her eyes" pictures her face going guarded, like a door shutting on a secret.

items.prompt: Which of these can the narrator NOT tell us for certain?
choices: What the note on the table said
How Lola felt inside during her classes
What the teacher said about Lola
items.why: The narrator was not in the classes and only hears about them from the teacher. Lola's feelings are never given directly; we see her only from the outside.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the text BEST supports the idea that Lola kept the class a secret?
choices: "She told no one in the family."
"Six months later a birthday card arrived for me."
items.why: "Told no one in the family" states the secrecy directly. Her age, the card, and the handwriting do not show that she hid the class.

items.prompt: "She was seventy-one when she enrolled in the barangay's adult literacy class." What does enrolled mean?
items.why: The teacher later calls her "the most stubborn student she had ever had," so enrolling means she signed up as a student.

items.prompt: "...the barangay's adult literacy class." Based on the passage, what is literacy?
choices: The ability to read and write
items.why: The whole story is about a grandmother who "never learned to read," and in the class she worked until "each day's letters stayed in her head." The class teaches reading and writing.

items.prompt: "Stubborn, she explained, in the best way: she refused to leave the room until each day's letters stayed in her head." What does stubborn mean in this use?
items.why: The teacher redefines stubborn with an example of refusing to give up, so here it means persistent.

items.prompt: "The letters leaning like trees in a wind." Why did the writer use this image?
choices: To say the card was written outdoors
To describe the weather on the narrator's birthday
To say the letters were green
To show the handwriting was unsteady but still standing, like someone new at writing
items.why: The simile pictures slanted, uneven letters while hinting at effort against resistance.

items.prompt: Which sentence BEST supports the idea that learning to read changed what Lola and the narrator could share?
choices: "I have received better-looking cards since then."
"It said: 'To my apo. Now I can read your notes. Love, Lola.'"
"She signed documents with a careful, looping mark."
items.why: The card says plainly that she can now read the narrator's notes, the very thing she could not do in the Marvin incident. The other sentences describe handwriting or the past.

items.prompt: Why does the narrator say "I have never received a braver one" instead of "a prettier one"?
choices: The narrator values the courage behind the card more than how it looks.
The card was actually very pretty.
items.why: The sentence contrasts better-looking cards with this braver one, showing what matters to the narrator.
